title: Cookies and Web Storage
summary: Four browser storage mechanisms, one real decision: cookies ride along on every request automatically, everything else doesn't. That single fact drives where you put session state, auth tokens, and everything in between.

slides.markdown:
Four storage mechanisms live in the browser — cookies, `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, `IndexedDB` — and picking the wrong one is a recurring source of both bugs and security incidents, not just inconvenience.

The axis that actually matters isn't "which one is newest" or "which one has the biggest quota" — it's **who gets to read it automatically**. Cookies are sent by the browser on every matching request without your code doing anything; the other three are inert until JavaScript explicitly reads them. That one distinction is the entire reason "where do you store an auth token" is a real interview question with a real wrong answer.

This topic covers each mechanism's actual lifetime and scope, then the storage decision that gets asked about most: tokens.

At a glance, before the details:

- **Cookies** — small (~4KB), sent automatically with every matching HTTP request. Built for the server to maintain state across requests before JS storage APIs existed.
- **localStorage** — a synchronous key-value store, persists indefinitely, scoped per-origin, never sent to the server automatically.
- **sessionStorage** — same API as localStorage, but scoped to one tab and cleared when that tab closes.
- **IndexedDB** — an asynchronous, transactional object database, built for structured data and much larger quotas (hundreds of MB, browser-dependent).

The first three are all designed for small amounts of data; IndexedDB is the only one meant for anything resembling "real" client-side data storage — an offline product catalog, cached API responses, or a local-first app's dataset.

A cookie is more than a name-value pair — its attributes decide who can read it and when it's sent: - **`HttpOnly`** — invisible to JavaScript (`document.cookie` won't show it), only readable by the server. The single most important defense against a cookie being stolen via XSS. - **`Secure`** — only sent over HTTPS, never plain HTTP. - **`SameSite`** — controls cross-site sending: `Strict` (never sent cross-site, even from a top-level link click), `Lax` (sent on top-level navigation like clicking a link, not on cross-site ``/fetch — the current browser default), `None` (sent everywhere, requires `Secure`). - **Expiry** — a session cookie (no `Max-Age`/`Expires`) dies when the browser closes; a persistent cookie survives until its set expiry. `SameSite=Lax` as a default (shipped by Chrome in 2020) is itself a major CSRF mitigation — it's why plain CSRF via a forged cross-site form submission got meaningfully harder without any app code changing at all.

slides.subTitle: Lifetime, scope, and a real cost
slides.markdown:
Same API (`.getItem`, `.setItem`, `.removeItem`), genuinely different lifetimes: **localStorage** persists until explicitly cleared — surviving browser restarts, tab closes, days or years; **sessionStorage** is scoped to a single tab and dies when that tab closes, and critically, a duplicated tab or a link opened in a new tab does **not** inherit the same sessionStorage — each tab gets its own.

Both are **synchronous** APIs, which is a real cost most people miss: a large `localStorage` read or write blocks the main thread, unlike `IndexedDB`'s async API. Storing a large JSON blob and reading it on every page load is a genuine, measurable performance cost, not just a theoretical one — synchronous localStorage access is explicitly called out as a main-thread bottleneck in browser performance guidance.

Both are also per-**origin**, not per-page — every page on `https://example.com` shares the same localStorage, regardless of path.

slides.subTitle: IndexedDB
slides.markdown:
IndexedDB solves what the others can't: **structured, queryable, large-volume** client-side data. It stores JS objects directly (no manual JSON stringify/parse), supports indexes for querying by a field other than the primary key, and runs **transactionally** — a set of writes either all commit or none do.

It's also the storage layer service workers reach for when caching structured data beyond what the Cache API's request/response pairs are built for — an offline-capable app storing a product catalog, or a note-taking app storing thousands of documents locally, uses IndexedDB, not localStorage, precisely because localStorage's ~5-10MB quota and synchronous API can't support that scale.

The cost is API complexity — raw IndexedDB's callback-based API is notoriously verbose, which is why most real usage goes through a wrapper library (Dexie.js, `idb`) rather than the raw API directly.

slides.sectionTitle: Why cookies alone ride along automatically
slides.markdown:
This is the fact everything else in this topic builds toward: **cookies are the only storage mechanism the browser attaches to a request without any JavaScript running.** `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, and `IndexedDB` are all inert data at rest — a server never sees them unless your code explicitly reads them and puts the value in a header or body.

That automatic attachment is a double-edged design. It's what makes cookie-based sessions simple — the server just checks the incoming cookie header, no client code needed to "remember" to attach anything. It's also exactly what makes cookies vulnerable to **CSRF**: a malicious site can trigger a request to your bank's domain, and the browser will happily attach your bank's session cookie to it, because the browser doesn't check who *initiated* the request, only which domain it's addressed to.

Storage mechanisms that require explicit JS to attach data avoid CSRF entirely, for exactly the reverse reason — but that same explicitness reopens the door to a different vulnerability class: XSS.

slides.sectionTitle: Storing a JWT in localStorage vs a cookie
slides.subTitle: The XSS/CSRF trade-off
slides.markdown:
This is the classic frontend security trade-off, and there's no option that's simply "safe" — each choice trades one attack surface for another.

**localStorage** — immune to CSRF (nothing attaches it automatically), but any successful **XSS** on your page can read it directly via `localStorage.getItem`, and exfiltrate the token in full, with no special effort. A single vulnerable third-party script is enough.

**An HttpOnly cookie** — immune to being read by JS at all, even from a successful XSS, which is the strongest defense against **token theft**. But it's automatically attached to every request to that domain, including ones a malicious site tricks the browser into making — **CSRF** — unless mitigated with `SameSite` and/or a CSRF token.

The practical consensus for production auth: **HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite=Strict/Lax cookies**, with a separate CSRF token for state-changing requests if `SameSite` alone isn't judged sufficient. This beats localStorage specifically because XSS-based token theft tends to be the more severe, less mitigable failure mode — full account takeover versus a forgeable request that `SameSite` already blocks most of. Deeper coverage of both attack classes lives in the `web-security` group.

slides.sectionTitle: Answering "where would you store an auth token"
slides.markdown:
A complete answer names the trade-off, not just a preference:

1. **Default recommendation:** an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict`, if your flows allow it) cookie, set by the server on login. JavaScript never touches the token directly.
2. **Why not localStorage:** it's the simpler implementation, but any XSS on the page is a full token compromise, with no additional exploit needed beyond getting a script to run.
3. **The cost you're accepting instead:** cookie-based auth reopens CSRF, which you mitigate with `SameSite` plus, for anything sensitive, an explicit CSRF token on state-changing requests.
4. **Where localStorage is genuinely fine:** non-sensitive data — UI preferences, a draft form's autosave, feature flags a user has toggled — where a leak has no real consequence.

Saying "cookie, HttpOnly, and here's what I still have to defend against" reads as someone who's shipped this decision before, not someone repeating a rule they memorized.

All of these have limits, and hitting them fails in different ways worth knowing:

- **localStorage/sessionStorage** — throw a synchronous `QuotaExceededError` on `setItem` once the ~5-10MB (browser-dependent) limit is hit; there's no automatic eviction, the write simply fails and your code must catch it.
- **IndexedDB** — quota is far larger and tied to available disk space, but under severe device storage pressure the browser can **evict an entire origin's storage** without warning ("best-effort" storage, versus "persistent" storage granted via the Storage API's `navigator.storage.persist()`).
- **Cookies** — a `Set-Cookie` past the ~4KB single-cookie limit, or past roughly 50 cookies per domain (limits vary by browser), is silently dropped or truncated by the browser, with no JS-visible error at all.

That last point is the sharpest gotcha: a server setting an oversized cookie gets no error anywhere — the cookie just silently fails to be stored, and the bug surfaces only as "the session isn't persisting," far from its actual cause.
